coverage.title: US suspends consular activities in Mexicali over threat
coverage.summary: The US Consulate in Tijuana instructed personnel to suspend activity and travel in Mexicali, directing staff and citizens to avoid government buildings and monitor surroundings in response to an unspecified threat.

events.background: The US Consulate in Tijuana oversees consular services across Baja California, including Mexicali, a major border crossing where Mexican authorities seized 4 million fentanilo doses the week before with DEA coordination.
events.view: A suspension signals the consulate assessed a direct threat serious enough to interrupt visa processing and official movement in a major trade crossing. The practical consequence is delays for US citizens seeking entry documents and disruption to routine diplomatic engagement at a border city of economic importance, though the alert does not disclose the threat's nature or duration.
events.prediction: The consulate will either resume operations within days if the threat is contained or clarified, or issue a travel advisory upgrade if conditions worsen. Observable evidence would be a formal status update from the US State Department naming the threat type or confirming the all-clear.

coverage.title: Mexico's Judiciary reforms transparency and public information rules
coverage.summary: The Judicial Administration Board has amended its transparency and public-information agreement, a formal action published in the Official Federal Gazette.

events.background: Mexico's judicial system underwent fundamental restructuring in 2024, replacing appointment with election for much of the federal judiciary, the new Supreme Court took office in September 2025, and practical tests now center on case resolution speed, enforcement, and independence when government or powerful interests are involved.
events.view: The amendment formalizes transparency and data-protection procedures for the reformed judiciary. Publication in the Official Federal Gazette makes the new rules binding on federal courts. The substance of the changes is not disclosed in available sources, so the practical effect on case disclosure, financial filings, or judicial independence cannot be determined from this announcement alone.
events.prediction: Courts will apply the revised rules to information requests and personnel records immediately. Whether the amendment strengthens or weakens public access depends on specific provisions not yet detailed in public reporting, that detail will emerge when transparency organizations or media test the new procedures against specific cases or records requests.

events.background: Sinaloa's constitution requires Congress to appoint an interim governor when an absence lasts more than 30 days. The appointment requires an absolute majority.
events.view: The second leave turns a brief return into a longer succession decision. If Congress appoints someone through October 2027, that person, not Rocha, will run the state while the US case proceeds.

events.background: Mexico's election agency audits how parties receive and spend money. Its online system is where parties record income and expenses. The documents cited by Mexico Against Corruption show that payments were made. They do not by themselves show why recipients were chosen.
events.view: The MX$134.9 million total covered 252,901 payments, about MX$533 each. The unresolved question is accounting. The investigation says it could not find the amount in Morena's filings, which warrants an official explanation but does not establish vote-buying.

coverage.title: Mexico's farm council challenges preliminary US strawberry duties
coverage.summary: The US Commerce Department's preliminary dumping margin averages 4.83% for winter strawberries from Mexico. A final decision is due January 8, 2027, and Mexico's farm council says the method could extend to other seasonal produce.

events.background: Antidumping cases have two separate tests: the Commerce Department estimates whether imports were sold below fair value, and the US International Trade Commission decides whether the domestic industry was injured. A preliminary margin is not the final result.
events.view: The immediate cost is narrower than the farm council's warning. The case applies to winter strawberries, and the 4.83% average is well below the 18.32% alleged at the start. Any broader precedent depends on the final reasoning, not only the rate.
events.prediction: Watch the Commerce Department's final determination on January 8, followed by the injury decision. Lower or zero final margins would weaken the case. Similar margins and a final injury finding would put the duties on firmer ground.

coverage.title: Manufacturing employment edges up 0.1% in June after four monthly declines
coverage.summary: The increase ended a four-month slide, but factory employment remained below a year earlier for a 40th consecutive month. Computer-equipment manufacturing was the exception.

events.background: INEGI's manufacturing survey tracks payroll employment across the factory sector. A 0.1% monthly rise shows that June was better than May, but it does not erase 40 straight months of year-over-year declines.
events.view: The split matters more than the small monthly gain. Factory hiring is still weak across the sector, while computer equipment is growing with demand for data-center hardware. That is a narrow pocket of strength, not a broad manufacturing recovery.
events.prediction: Watch the July survey for another monthly increase and fewer year-over-year losses across industries. If computer equipment remains the main exception, the recovery is still narrow.

coverage.title: US money-transfer rule near Mexico border damages small businesses
coverage.summary: The Trump administration's April rule targeting cartel money-laundering has caused unintended economic harm to legitimate small companies along the US-Mexico border, affecting business operations and cash flows.

events.background: FinCEN's March 2025 order covered cash transactions above $200 and below $10,000 at selected border money businesses. The agency later raised the minimum to $1,000. A federal appeals court said one store estimated 14 extra reporting hours a day and lost 50-60% of customers during the rule's first week.
events.view: The court record shows a real compliance burden, but the evidence centers on one business and the injunction covers only Southern California. It does not prove that every border business suffered the same harm or measure whether the reports stopped money laundering.
events.prediction: Watch whether FinCEN extends or changes the current order after September 2, 2026. If Treasury raises the threshold or a court broadens the injunction, the burden would shrink. A renewed order with the same terms would preserve it.
